title: Deep in one: Hebrews
for: I want to see how Jesus fulfils the Old Testament
subtitle: Thirteen sessions, one for each chapter of Hebrews: the angels, Moses, the priesthood and the sacrifices read in the light of Christ, and how to read the Old Testament the way this sermon does.
intro: This track reads the letter to the Hebrews a chapter at a sitting, thirteen sessions in all. Hebrews has no greeting and no named author. Its writer calls it a word of exhortation, and it reads like a sermon sent by post to believers who had once suffered bravely and were now tired, drifting and tempted to give up on Christ. Its answer is not a scolding. It is a long look at who Jesus is.

Hebrews takes the great gifts of Israel's faith one by one, the prophets, the angels, Moses, the land, the priesthood, the tabernacle, the covenant and the sacrifices, and shows each as a true shadow of something it could not itself give. Read slowly, it teaches you to read the whole Old Testament in the light of Christ. Each session takes about fifteen minutes and ends with one question, one thing to do, one verse to keep and a guide for a group.

about: This guide is for anyone leading a small group through Deep in one: Hebrews. The group reads one chapter a meeting, thirteen in all. Hebrews is a sustained argument built almost entirely from the Old Testament, so the group will keep turning back to Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, the Psalms and Jeremiah. That is the point. By the end, the group should be able to open an Old Testament passage and ask how it points to Christ without forcing it.

Each person reads the chapter, its notes and the session before the group meets. The meeting reads part of the chapter aloud and talks it over, using the group guide for that session, which is gathered below in order with the page each session opens and the question it asks.

sections.title: The group
body: Four to ten people is a good size, small enough that everyone speaks. Meet for about seventy-five minutes, once a week, for thirteen meetings, and keep the end time you promised. A group that meets once a fortnight can take two chapters together where the argument runs on, such as chapters 9 and 10 on the sacrifices. A leader doesn't need to be a scholar. A leader needs to have read the chapter and its notes, and to be willing to say plainly when they don't know.

sections.title: The room
body: Sit where everyone can see each other, with the text open in front of everyone, in print or on a phone. Hebrews quotes the Old Testament on almost every page, so ask one person each week to have the quoted passage open in its own place and read it aloud when the group reaches it. Make it plain at the first meeting that anyone may pass on any question, that what people say about their own lives stays in the room, and that no one has to pray aloud.

sections.title: The order of a meeting
body: About seventy-five minutes, in this order. Keep to the times loosely and to the end time strictly.
steps: Ten minutes: the opening question, once round the circle. Anyone may pass.
Fifteen minutes: one person reads the heart of the chapter aloud, and another reads the Old Testament passage it quotes in its own place.
Thirty-five minutes: the three questions to talk over, in order. Ask where each answer is in the text.
Five minutes: one person reads the verse to keep, and the group says what it noticed in it.
Five minutes: the prayer prompt, in your own words.
Five minutes: name the next chapter and the page its session opens, and say when you will meet.

sections.title: When a hard question comes
body: Hebrews has some of the most argued-over warnings in the Bible, above all in chapters 6 and 10. Christians in the Reformed, Wesleyan, Catholic and Orthodox traditions read them differently, and the notes set out each reading without choosing. So should the group. Give each view in the form its own holders would sign, and don't settle for the group what the churches have not settled. Whether a believer can finally fall away divides faithful churches without dividing the faith.

Watch also for a misreading the notes refuse. When Hebrews calls the first covenant old or a shadow, it is not passing judgment on the Jewish people or calling Israel's worship false. A shadow is real and has the true shape of what casts it. If the conversation slides toward contempt, read the note on 8:7-13 together.

sections.title: When someone is hurting
body: Hebrews was written to tired people, and some in the group will be tired in the same way: worn out by suffering, by doubt or by years of holding on. Others will be frightened by the warnings and afraid that they have gone too far. When someone says so, stop and listen. Thank them, don't explain their suffering for them, and remember that fear of having fallen away is not usually the mark of someone who has.

Some passages have been misused to wound people: the warnings used to frighten the anxious, the Father's discipline in chapter 12 used to excuse a parent's cruelty, the call to obey leaders in chapter 13 used to shield abuse. The notes refuse every one of those uses, and so should the group. If someone says that anyone is harming them or a child, take it seriously and don't promise to keep it secret.

sections.title: When to point someone to Find Help
body: Point someone to Find Help when what they carry has become too heavy to set down: fear or guilt that will not let them rest, grief that has taken their sleep or appetite for weeks, harm done to them at home or in a church, or any sign that they no longer want to be alive. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, and its lines for help right now are open day and night. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number. A leader is a friend in that moment, not a counsellor.

sessions.title: God has spoken in his Son
teaching: Hebrews begins without a greeting, like a sermon. Its first sentence sets the whole Old Testament in one frame: “On many past occasions and in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets. But in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son” (Hebrews 1:1-2). The earlier words were not wrong. They were partial, spoken in pieces. The Son is the word they were leading to, the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of his nature.

Then the writer compares the Son with the angels, using a chain of quotations from the Psalms and the prophets. Why angels? Jewish tradition held that the law at Sinai was given through angels, and Stephen and Paul both say so. To show the Son above the angels is to show him above the most glorious way God had spoken before. No one knows who wrote this. Origen, in the third century, judged that only God knows, and most scholars still agree.

open.label: Hebrews 1, passage by passage
open.why: God speaking in his Son, the angels worshipping him, and the Psalms the writer quotes, each explained in plain words.

also.label: Hebrews in the Study Bible
also.why: Who might have written Hebrews, to whom and when, how its argument is built, and why the church received it as Scripture.

also.label: The book of Hebrews
also.why: The whole sermon in short pictures, so you can see the shape of the argument before you read it a chapter at a time.

also.label: The Septuagint and Scripture
also.why: Hebrews quotes the Greek translation of the Old Testament, and this guide explains why its wording sometimes differs from your English Bible.

sessions.question: Hebrews says God spoke in many ways and now has spoken in his Son. What difference does it make to read the Old Testament as a word that was leading somewhere?
sessions.do: Read Hebrews 1:1-4 slowly and list everything it says about the Son. Then look up Psalm 110:1, quoted at the end of the chapter, and read the whole psalm.

verse.text: On many past occasions and in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets. But in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son, whom He appointed heir of all things, and through whom He made the universe.

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Has a later part of a story ever made you understand an earlier part differently?
discuss: The writer says God spoke in many ways through the prophets. Which of those ways do you know from the Old Testament?
Why might it matter to tired believers that God's last word is a Son and not a new set of instructions?
The Son is called the exact representation of God's nature. If you want to know what God is like, where does that send you?
group.pray: Give thanks in your own words that God has spoken and not stayed silent, and ask to hear the Son clearly in every part of Scripture.

sessions.title: Do not drift; he became like us
teaching: The first of the book's warnings comes early and is gentle: pay closer attention, so that we do not drift away. Drift is not rebellion. It is what happens to a boat no one is steering. Then the writer turns to Psalm 8, which asks what man is that God is mindful of him and says all things are put under his feet. We don't yet see everything under humanity's feet. But we see Jesus, made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory because he suffered death for everyone.

Here Hebrews reads a psalm about the human calling and finds it fulfilled in the one true man. He shared our flesh and blood so that by his death he might break the power of the devil and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by the fear of death. He is not ashamed to call us brothers and sisters. He had to be made like us in every way to become a merciful and faithful high priest.

open.label: Hebrews 2, passage by passage
open.why: The first warning, Psalm 8 and the Son made lower than the angels, and the one who shared our flesh and blood, explained in plain words.

also.label: The incarnation in the whole Bible
also.why: What it means that the Son of God became a man, traced from the promises of the prophets to the Gospels and this chapter.

also.label: Follow a verse
also.why: Follow Hebrews 2 back to Psalm 8 and see how the writer reads a psalm about every human being as a psalm about Jesus.

sessions.question: Hebrews says Jesus frees those held all their lives by the fear of death. Where does that fear shape your choices, even quietly?
sessions.do: Read Psalm 8 in its own place, then read Hebrews 2:5-9 again. Write one sentence on what the psalm says about every human being and one on what Hebrews sees in it.

verse.text: Because He Himself suffered when He was tempted, He is able to help those who are being tempted.

care: If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, or you feel you do not want to go on, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. You do not have to carry it alone. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is something you drifted away from without ever deciding to?
discuss: Why do you think the writer warns about drifting before he warns about anything worse?
Psalm 8 is about humanity, and Hebrews reads it about Jesus. Is that a fair reading of the psalm? Why or why not?
Jesus is not ashamed to call us his brothers and sisters. What would change if you believed that this week?
group.pray: Pray in your own words for anyone in the group who feels themselves drifting, and give thanks that Jesus shared our flesh and blood.

sessions.title: Moses the servant, Jesus the Son
teaching: Moses was the greatest figure in Israel's memory, and Hebrews doesn't belittle him. Moses was faithful in all God's house. But he was faithful as a servant, testifying to what would be spoken later, and Jesus is faithful as the Son over the house. The comparison honours both. The servant built well, and the house was always meant for the Son.

Then the writer quotes Psalm 95, which looks back on the generation Moses led out of Egypt. They saw the sea part and still hardened their hearts in the wilderness, and they did not enter the land. The psalm says Today, if you hear his voice, and Hebrews takes that word seriously: as long as it is still called today, the invitation is open. This is a habit of the writer worth learning. He reads an old psalm as God speaking now, to his own readers, and he asks them to encourage one another daily so that none of them is hardened.

open.label: Hebrews 3, passage by passage
open.why: Moses the servant and Jesus the Son, Psalm 95 and the generation in the wilderness, and the call to encourage one another daily.

also.label: The rescue from Egypt
also.why: The part of the Bible's story Hebrews is reading here: the exodus, Sinai and the years in the wilderness that Psalm 95 remembers.

also.label: The exodus
also.why: Short pictures of the rescue from Egypt, so the generation in the wilderness is a story you can see and not only a warning.

sessions.question: The wilderness generation had seen miracles and still hardened their hearts. What hardens a heart slowly, without anyone noticing?
sessions.do: Read Psalm 95 in its own place, then Numbers 14:1-11. Name one person this week you can encourage while it is still called today, and do it.

verse.text: But exhort one another daily, as long as it is called today, so that none of you may be hardened by sin’s deceitfulness.

care: If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Who encouraged you at a time when you needed it most?
discuss: Hebrews honours Moses and puts Jesus above him. How can you honour the Old Testament while reading it in the light of Christ?
The writer treats the word today in Psalm 95 as spoken to his readers. What does that teach you about how to read the psalms?
The cure for a hard heart in this chapter is other people. Why do you think it isn't something you can do alone?
group.pray: Pray in your own words for each person in the group by name, that none of you would be hardened, and give thanks for those who encourage you.

sessions.title: A rest that remains
teaching: Chapter 4 follows a thread from the first page of the Bible to the last. God rested on the seventh day. He promised Israel rest in the land, and Joshua led them in. But centuries later Psalm 95 still speaks of entering God's rest, so the writer reasons that Joshua's rest was not the final one. There remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God. The land was real, and it was also a picture of something larger: rest with God himself.

Then two pictures close the chapter. The word of God is living and sharper than any sword, and nothing is hidden from it. That could be frightening. But the next sentence turns it: we have a great high priest who has gone through the heavens, who sympathizes with our weaknesses, tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin. So the one who sees everything is also the one who understands, and we can come to the throne of grace with confidence.

open.label: Hebrews 4, passage by passage
open.why: The promise of rest, the Sabbath rest that remains, the living word, and the high priest who understands, each explained in plain words.

also.label: The Sabbath in the whole Bible
also.why: God's rest on the seventh day, the command at Sinai, and how the New Testament speaks of rest after Christ, traced through Scripture.

also.label: The land and the judges
also.why: Joshua and the rest in the land, the part of the story Hebrews says pointed beyond itself to a rest that still remains.

also.label: Rest and the Sabbath
also.why: What it looks like to practise rest in an ordinary week as a confession that the world is held by God and not by you.

sessions.question: Hebrews says the God who sees everything is also the high priest who sympathizes. Which of those two do you find harder to believe, and why?
sessions.do: Set aside one stretch of time this week, even an hour, to stop working and rest on purpose. Begin it by reading Hebrews 4:14-16 aloud.

verse.text: Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need.

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: When did you last feel truly rested, and what made it possible?
discuss: The land was a real rest and also a picture of a greater one. What other Old Testament gifts might work the same way?
Why do you think the writer puts the sharp word of God and the sympathetic high priest side by side?
What keeps people from coming to God with confidence, and what in this chapter answers it?
group.pray: Bring to God in your own words one weakness each of you carries, trusting that he understands, and ask for grace in your time of need.

sessions.title: A high priest from among us
teaching: A priest in Israel stood between the people and God. He was taken from among the people, so he could deal gently with those who go astray, and he did not appoint himself; God called him, as he called Aaron. Hebrews says Jesus fits both marks. God called him in the words of two psalms, one naming him Son and the other a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek. And he was taken from among us, more deeply than any priest before him.

The proof is one of the most startling verses in the New Testament. During his earthly life Jesus offered up prayers with loud cries and tears to the one who could save him from death, and he was heard. Although he was a Son, he learned obedience through what he suffered. Then the writer stops and scolds his hearers gently: they ought to be teachers by now, and they still need milk. The chapter is a call to grow up.

open.label: Hebrews 5, passage by passage
open.why: What makes a high priest, the Son called by God, the prayers with loud cries and tears, and the readers still on milk.

also.label: Hebrews 5, the guided walk
also.why: Seven steps through the chapter, so that you see for yourself how the writer builds his case before you read anyone's comment on it.

also.label: Prophet, priest and king
also.why: The three offices of Israel and how the New Testament sees Jesus fulfil each, so the priesthood is seen beside the others.

sessions.question: Jesus prayed with loud cries and tears and was heard. What does that tell you about the prayers you have been afraid to pray?
sessions.do: Read Leviticus 16:1-6 to see what an earthly high priest had to do for himself before he could serve the people. Then read Hebrews 5:1-10 again and note what is the same and what is different.

verse.text: During the days of Jesus’ earthly life, He offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard because of His reverence.

care: If you are praying with tears and wondering whether you are heard, this verse is for you. The Son of God prayed that way too. The psalms are full of such prayers, and God kept them in his book. If your nights are full of tears now, please do not carry it alone. Tell someone you trust: a doctor, a pastor or a friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Who in your life deals gently with people who get things wrong?
discuss: A priest had to be taken from among the people. Why does it matter that Jesus is one of us and not only above us?
What do you make of the words that the Son learned obedience through what he suffered?
The writer says his readers should be teachers by now. What is the difference between milk and solid food in your own faith?
group.pray: Bring your own unspoken prayers to God in your own words, and give thanks that Jesus prayed with tears and was heard.

sessions.title: The sharpest warning, and an anchor
teaching: Chapter 6 holds the sharpest warning in the book. It is impossible, the writer says, for those who have been enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, shared in the Holy Spirit and then fallen away, to be restored to repentance. Christians read this in more than one way, and each view deserves its strongest form. Many in the Reformed and Baptist world hold that these people had real experiences of the gospel among believers but were never born again, or that God uses such warnings to keep his people holding on. Many Wesleyan and Arminian Christians read it as describing real believers who can be lost by settled unbelief. Catholic and Orthodox teaching holds that grace can be lost through grave sin and restored by repentance.

Whatever the reading, two things are plain. The warning is about turning against Christ himself, not about ordinary failure. And the writer's aim is to keep his readers safe, so in the next breath he says he is convinced of better things in their case, and he ends with God's oath and a hope that is an anchor for the soul.

open.label: Hebrews 6, passage by passage
open.why: Going on to maturity, the sharpest warning with every main reading set out without choosing, and God's oath as an anchor for the soul.

also.label: Can you lose your salvation?
also.why: The main views on whether a believer can finally fall away, each stated so its own holders would recognise it.

also.label: Perseverance in the whole Bible
also.why: What Scripture says about God keeping his people and his people holding on, read across the canon and not from one verse.

also.label: Where Christians differ
also.why: The questions that divide faithful churches without dividing the faith, set side by side, so that this chapter is read in good company.

sessions.question: The writer warns sharply and then says he is convinced of better things in your case. Which of those two do you most need to hear this week?
sessions.do: Read Hebrews 6:13-20 twice. Draw an anchor and write on it, in your own words, the two unchangeable things the writer says hold it fast.

verse.text: We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure.

care: If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Have you ever been warned by someone who plainly loved you? How did it feel?
discuss: Set out the main readings of 6:4-6 as fairly as you can. What does each one protect that the others might lose?
All the readings agree the warning is about turning against Christ himself. Why does that distinction matter for anxious readers?
Why do you think the writer follows his hardest warning with God's oath and an anchor?
group.pray: Pray in your own words for anyone in the group who is afraid, and give thanks for the hope that holds when your own grip is weak.

sessions.title: A priest like Melchizedek
teaching: Melchizedek appears in Genesis 14 for three verses. He is king of Salem and priest of God Most High, he brings Abraham bread and wine and blesses him, and Abraham gives him a tenth. Then he disappears, until Psalm 110 says of the coming king, “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4). Hebrews puts the two passages together. Scripture gives Melchizedek no genealogy, no birth and no death, and the writer reads that silence as a picture of the Son.

The argument is careful. If the Levitical priesthood had made people perfect, why would God speak centuries later of another priest, from another order? Jesus came from Judah, not Levi. He is a priest not by family descent but by the power of an indestructible life, and God confirmed it with an oath. The old priests died and had to be replaced. This one always lives to intercede for those who draw near through him.

open.label: Hebrews 7, passage by passage
open.why: Melchizedek king of righteousness, greater than Abraham and Levi, a change of priesthood, and a priest who always lives to intercede.

also.label: Abraham and the promise
also.why: Where Abraham's meeting with Melchizedek stands in the whole story, from the call out of Ur to the promise to bless every nation.

also.label: The Messiah in the whole Bible
also.why: How the promised king of the Psalms and the prophets is traced to Jesus, including the priest-king of Psalm 110.

sessions.question: Jesus always lives to intercede for those who come to God through him. What would you want to know he is praying for you today?
sessions.do: Read Genesis 14:17-20 and Psalm 110 in their own places. Then write a short list of what Hebrews draws from each, and notice what it draws from what the text leaves unsaid.

verse.text: Therefore He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them.

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Who has prayed for you faithfully, perhaps without your knowing at the time?
discuss: Hebrews makes much of what Genesis does not say about Melchizedek. Is that a fair way to read? What keeps it from becoming guesswork?
Why does it matter that Jesus' priesthood rests on an indestructible life and not on family descent?
What difference does it make to your prayers to believe that Jesus is already interceding?
group.pray: Pray in your own words for one another, by name, and give thanks that Jesus prays for each of you before you pray at all.

sessions.title: A better covenant
teaching: Chapter 8 tells us its own main point: we have a high priest seated at God's right hand, serving in the true sanctuary. The tabernacle Moses built was made to the pattern shown him on the mountain, and Hebrews calls it a copy and shadow of what is in heaven. A shadow is not false. It has the true shape of the thing that casts it. Israel met God there truly, and learned there that sin is serious and that God provides the way back.

Then the writer quotes Jeremiah 31, the prophet's promise of a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, written not on stone but on hearts: “I will be their God, and they will be My people” (Jeremiah 31:33). If God calls one covenant new, the writer reasons, the first has become the older one. He is not passing judgment on the Jewish people. He is reading a Jewish prophet, and putting the fault where Jeremiah put it, in the people's failure to keep the covenant, not in God's law.

open.label: Hebrews 8, passage by passage
open.why: The main point of the argument, copy and shadow, and Jeremiah's new covenant, with what the word obsolete does and does not mean.

also.label: Covenant
also.why: Short pictures of God binding himself to his people, from Noah and Abraham to Sinai, David and the new covenant in Jesus' blood.

also.label: How the covenants fit together
also.why: The main ways Christians understand how the old covenant and the new relate, each set out by its own best defenders.

also.label: Covenant and treaty
also.why: What a covenant was in the ancient world, so that God's promises to Israel are heard as their first hearers heard them.

sessions.question: Jeremiah promised a law written on the heart. What is the difference between keeping a rule and having it written on you?
sessions.do: Read Jeremiah 31:31-34 in its own place, then Hebrews 8:8-12. Underline the four promises of the new covenant and choose the one you most need to believe this week.

verse.text: For this is the covenant I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord. I will put My laws in their minds and inscribe them on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they will be My people.

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is a promise someone made to you that shaped your life?
discuss: A shadow is real and has the true shape of what casts it. How does that picture help you read the tabernacle and the sacrifices?
How has the word obsolete in 8:13 been misread, and how does reading Jeremiah's own words protect against that?
Christians differ on how the covenants fit together. What do the views share, and where do they part?
group.pray: Give thanks in your own words for the promises of the new covenant, and pray for Jewish friends and neighbours with respect and love.

sessions.title: Blood and a clean conscience
teaching: Chapter 9 walks through the tabernacle room by room. In the outer room the priests served daily. Into the inner room, the Most Holy Place, only the high priest went, once a year on the Day of Atonement, and never without blood for himself and for the people. The writer says the Holy Spirit was showing something by that arrangement: the way in was not yet open, and the gifts and sacrifices could not make the worshipper's conscience clean.

Then Christ enters, not into a tent made with hands, but into heaven itself, and not with the blood of goats and calves but with his own. Blood in Scripture means life given up. Hebrews argues that if the old sacrifices made the body ceremonially clean, how much more will the blood of Christ purify our consciences, so that we may serve the living God. He was offered once to bear the sins of many, and he will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to bring salvation.

open.label: Hebrews 9, passage by passage
open.why: The tabernacle and the Day of Atonement, Christ's own blood, the covenant brought into force by a death, and his second appearing.

also.label: Why blood?
also.why: Short pictures of why the Bible speaks so much of blood, from Abel and the Passover to the altar and the cross.

also.label: Offerings and purity
also.why: What the offerings of Leviticus were and what clean and unclean meant, so that this chapter's argument has its ground under it.

also.label: The calendar and the festivals
also.why: Where the Day of Atonement fell in Israel's year and what happened on it, the day Hebrews reads in the light of the cross.

sessions.question: Hebrews says Christ's blood can cleanse a conscience. What would it mean for your conscience to be clean, not only quiet?
sessions.do: Read Leviticus 16 in one sitting, the Day of Atonement. Then read Hebrews 9:11-14 and write down three things Christ did that the high priest could not.

verse.text: how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God, purify our consciences from works of death, so that we may serve the living God!

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is something you were taught as a child that you only understood years later?
discuss: Why do you think the high priest could enter the Most Holy Place only once a year and only with blood?
Many people find the Bible's talk of blood strange or repellent. How would you explain it to someone who does?
The old sacrifices cleansed the body; Christ cleanses the conscience. What is the difference, and why does it matter?
group.pray: Give thanks in your own words for Christ's one offering, and bring to God anything that still troubles your conscience.

sessions.title: Once for all, so draw near
teaching: The law, Hebrews says, is only a shadow of the good things to come. The same sacrifices offered year after year could never take sins away; they were a yearly reminder of them. Then the writer hears Psalm 40 on Christ's lips: “Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but a body You prepared for Me” (Hebrews 10:5). He quotes the Greek translation, which reads a body where the Hebrew has ears, and either way the psalm says what God wanted was a life given in obedience. Every other priest stands daily. This priest offered one sacrifice for all time and sat down.

So the argument turns into an invitation. Since we have confidence to enter by the blood of Jesus, let us draw near, hold on to our hope, spur one another on, and not give up meeting together. Then comes another hard warning, against going on in sin deliberately after knowing the truth, and right after it a word of memory: remember the early days, when you suffered and stood firm.

open.label: Hebrews 10, passage by passage
open.why: The shadow and the reality, Psalm 40, the priest who sat down, the call to draw near, the fourth warning and the call to remember.

also.label: The Lamb
also.why: Short pictures of the lamb through the whole Bible, from Abraham's ram and the Passover to the Lamb on the throne.

also.label: The atonement in the whole Bible
also.why: The pictures Scripture uses for what the cross achieved, sacrifice, ransom, victory and substitution, and how they fit together.

also.label: Hard passages
also.why: Hebrews 10:26 is among the Bible's hard passages, and this page gathers the notes that take them up honestly, with care in reach.

sessions.question: Every other priest stood; this one sat down. What are you still trying to finish that Christ has already finished?
sessions.do: Read Hebrews 10:19-25 and list every let us. Choose one, and do it this week with someone in your church.

verse.text: Let us hold resolutely to the hope we profess, for He who promised is faithful.

care: If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
If you are suffering now, for your faith or for any other reason, you do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is something you used to do every year that only reminded you of what was still undone?
discuss: Why does it matter so much to the writer that Christ sat down?
The call to draw near comes with a call to meet together. Why do you think the writer joins them?
How would you explain the warning of 10:26-31 to someone afraid they have sinned too often to be forgiven?
group.pray: Give thanks in your own words that the sacrifice is finished, and pray for anyone you know who has stopped meeting with the church.

sessions.title: By faith
teaching: Chapter 11 is a walk through the whole Old Testament with one word in hand: “Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see” (Hebrews 11:1). Abel, Enoch and Noah. Abraham leaving home without knowing where he was going, Sarah laughing and then believing, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph. Moses choosing disgrace with God's people over the treasures of Egypt. Rahab. Then the names come too fast to tell: Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel and the prophets.

Notice two things. This is not a list of the flawless. Several of these names carry stories of real failure, and Hebrews honours them for trusting God, not for being impressive. And the chapter turns in the middle of verse 35. Some by faith shut the mouths of lions. Others by faith were tortured, imprisoned, killed. All of them died without receiving what was promised, looking for a city whose builder is God.

open.label: Hebrews 11, passage by passage
open.why: What faith is, Abel to Noah, Abraham and Sarah looking for a city, Moses and Rahab, and those who were rescued and those who were not.

also.label: Faith in the whole Bible
also.why: What Scripture means by faith, traced from Abraham to this chapter, so that trust is not confused with wishful thinking.

also.label: The Bible's timeline
also.why: Place each name in this chapter on the long line of the Old Testament and see how many centuries of trust the writer gathers in one breath.

sessions.question: Hebrews honours people who died without receiving what was promised. Whose faith in your own life looked like that?
sessions.do: Choose two names from Hebrews 11 you know least and read their stories in the Old Testament. Write a sentence on what their faith actually looked like, failures included.

verse.text: Instead, they were longing for a better country, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them.

care: If you have prayed for someone to be rescued, from illness, from danger, from prison, from death, and the rescue did not come, this chapter does not say your prayer was too weak. The three friends in Daniel said God was able to deliver them, “But even if He does not” (Daniel 3:18), they would still trust him. Grief and confusion at such a loss are not a lack of faith. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Whose name would you add to this chapter from your own family or church?
discuss: Faith is defined here as assurance about what we hope for. How is that different from wishful thinking?
Samson and Jephthah are in this list. What does that tell you about whom God honours?
Some were rescued by faith and some were killed by faith. How does the chapter keep both from being a measure of how much faith they had?
group.pray: Give thanks in your own words for the people of faith who went before you, and pray for those still waiting for what was promised.

sessions.title: The race and the city
teaching: Chapter 11 was a stadium filling with witnesses. Chapter 12 puts the reader on the track. Throw off what weighs you down, run with endurance, and fix your eyes on Jesus, who for the joy set before him endured the cross and sat down at the right hand of God. Then the writer reads Proverbs: the Lord disciplines the one he loves. Hardship is not proof that God has abandoned you. It can be training, the way a father trains a son.

The chapter ends with two mountains. Sinai burned with fire, darkness and storm, and even Moses trembled. But you have not come there. You have come to Mount Zion, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, to angels in joyful assembly, to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, and to sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel. Abel's blood cried out for justice. Jesus' blood speaks mercy. Still, our God is a consuming fire, and we receive a kingdom that cannot be shaken.

open.label: Hebrews 12, passage by passage
open.why: The race with eyes on Jesus, the Father's training, Esau's warning, Sinai and Zion, and the unshakable kingdom, each explained in plain words.

also.label: The new creation
also.why: The end of the Bible's story, the city of God come down, which Hebrews calls the heavenly Jerusalem the reader has already come to.

also.label: Themes of the Bible
also.why: Follow a theme such as the city or the kingdom through the books that speak of it, and see how Hebrews gathers it up.

sessions.question: Hebrews says you have come to Zion, not Sinai. Which mountain does your faith feel like it stands at right now, and why?
sessions.do: Read Exodus 19:16-25, the scene at Sinai, and then Hebrews 12:18-24. Write the two scenes side by side in two columns and read the second column aloud.

verse.text: Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.

care: What if ‘Father’ is a hard word for you? Some readers had a father who was absent, or who hurt them. If your own father was not there, or did not show you love, this passage is not asking you to picture him. It is telling you what you should have been shown, and what God is. If what happened to you still weighs on you, please talk with someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is the longest race or task of endurance you have ever finished?
discuss: What weighs runners down in the race of faith, and what is the difference between a weight and a sin?
How can hardship be training without making God the author of every wrong done to us?
Abel's blood cried out and Jesus' blood speaks a better word. What is that better word?
group.pray: Pray in your own words for anyone in the group who is weary, and fix your eyes together on Jesus, who finished the race.

sessions.title: Outside the camp
teaching: After twelve chapters of argument, Hebrews ends with ordinary life: keep loving one another, show hospitality to strangers, remember prisoners as if you were in prison with them, honour marriage, keep free from the love of money. The writer means these as the sacrifices that now please God, praise on the lips and good done with the hands. The great argument about priests and altars arrives at a kitchen table and a prison visit.

Then one last reading of the Old Testament. On the Day of Atonement the bodies of the animals were burned outside the camp. Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, so let us go to him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace he bore. Here we have no lasting city. We are looking for the one that is to come. The readers were tempted to go back inside, to what was familiar and safe. The writer asks them to go out, toward Jesus, because that is where he is.

open.label: Hebrews 13, passage by passage
open.why: Love in everyday life, remembering leaders, going outside the camp, the sacrifice of praise, and the God of peace, each explained in plain words.

also.label: How to show hospitality to outsiders
also.why: Hebrews 13 begins with strangers at the table. This guide makes that ordinary and possible in your own home.

also.label: The Nicene Creed
also.why: The church's confession of the Son as God from God and Light from Light, the faith Hebrews argued for in its first chapter.

also.label: Deep in one: Revelation
also.why: The next track on the road, in Deep in the New Testament: Deep in one: Revelation. Take it up when this one has settled.

sessions.question: The writer asks his readers to go to Jesus outside the camp. Where is the camp you are tempted to stay inside, and what would going out cost?
sessions.do: Choose one thing from Hebrews 13:1-6 you have not done in a long time, such as visiting someone in prison or inviting a stranger to eat, and do it before the month is out.

verse.text: For here we do not have a permanent city, but we are looking for the city that is to come.

care: If you have been harmed by a controlling leader or church, what was done was wrong, and it was not your fault. You are free to step away and to tell someone you trust. If you were abused in other ways, or a crime was done, it should be reported to the authorities. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Which of these thirteen sessions will you remember longest, and why?
discuss: Why might a book this full of argument end with hospitality, prisoners, marriage and money?
What does it mean today to bear the disgrace Jesus bore, and where have Christians confused that with simply being disliked?
Looking back over the whole book, which part of the Old Testament do you now read differently, and how?
group.pray: Give thanks in your own words for the great Shepherd of the sheep, and ask that each of you would go to him wherever he is found.
